lessonTitle: Reference Ranges and Sources of Error

blocks.text: A healthy 35-year-old is sent a routine screening panel of twenty blood tests and one result is flagged as abnormal. Nothing is wrong with her. The flag was not an error of the laboratory; it was a consequence of how reference ranges are built, and arithmetic shows it should be expected.

blocks.markdown: A laboratory result is meaningful only against a comparison. The usual comparison is a **reference interval**, derived by measuring the analyte in a large group of reference individuals selected as healthy and defining the limits that contain the central 95% of results. The interval is a statistical statement about a population, not a boundary between health and disease.

blocks.title: Reference interval
blocks.text: The reference interval is the range between the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of results from a healthy reference population. If results are approximately Gaussian (normal), it equals the mean plus or minus 1.96 standard deviations. Skewed analytes are handled by transforming the data or by directly using percentiles. By construction 5% of healthy people fall outside: 2.5% below and 2.5% above. Intervals vary with age, sex, method and laboratory, and each laboratory should state its own.

blocks.caption: x-bar is the mean and s the standard deviation of the healthy reference group (for approximately Gaussian data).

blocks.title: Deriving a reference interval
blocks.prompt: In a healthy reference group the serum concentration of an analyte is Gaussian with mean 4.2 mmol/L and standard deviation 0.30 mmol/L. Calculate the reference interval.
blocks.answer: The reference interval is about 3.6 to 4.8 mmol/L; 5% of healthy individuals lie outside it.

blocks.caption: For n independent tests in a healthy person, each with a 95% chance of being within range.

blocks.markdown: For n = 20 independent tests this gives 1 minus 0.95 to the power 20, which is about 64%. Most healthy people will therefore have a flagged result on a broad panel. A slightly abnormal result should be interpreted with the clinical picture and, if appropriate, repeated; it should not automatically trigger more investigation.

blocks.caption: Common pre-analytical causes of spurious results.

blocks.markdown: Most laboratory errors occur before the sample reaches the analyser (**pre-analytical**), followed by errors in the analysis itself and in reporting. A result that does not fit the clinical picture should prompt a question about the sample before any treatment: an implausible potassium with a normal ECG and normal kidney function, for example, suggests haemolysis or contamination.

blocks.title: Sensitivity, specificity and predictive value
blocks.prompt: A test is applied to 1000 people, of whom 50 have the disease. It is positive in 45 of them and in 95 of the 950 without the disease. Calculate the sensitivity, specificity and positive predictive value.

steps.text: PPV: true positives over all positives (45 plus 95 equals 140).

blocks.answer: Sensitivity 90%, specificity 90%, PPV about 32%: because the disease is uncommon, most positives are false.

blocks.title: Sensitivity, specificity and cut-off
blocks.text: Raising the cut-off for calling a test positive reduces false positives (higher specificity) but misses more cases (lower sensitivity). A highly sensitive test, when negative, helps rule disease out; a highly specific test, when positive, helps rule it in. Predictive values depend on prevalence.

points: Reference intervals contain the central 95% of a healthy population, so 5% of healthy people are flagged, and the chance of at least one flag rises quickly with the number of tests.
Pre-analytical errors such as haemolysis, delayed processing and EDTA contamination cause spurious results; suspect them when a result does not fit the clinical picture.
Sensitivity and specificity describe test performance; positive predictive value also depends on prevalence.

questions.stem: A reference interval in a clinical laboratory is usually defined as which of the following?

options.text: The central 95% of results in a healthy reference population
The range of values seen only in diseased patients
The mean plus or minus 3 standard deviations in all patients
The range of values in the last 10 patients tested

questions.correctOptionText: The central 95% of results in a healthy reference population

distractorRationale.b: Disease ranges are not reference intervals.
distractorRationale.c: Three standard deviations would contain about 99.7%.
distractorRationale.d: Reference groups must be defined, not just the latest patients.

questions.explanation: The interval is chosen so that 95% of healthy individuals fall inside, giving 2.5% in each tail. It describes a population and is not a threshold for disease.

questions.stem: A healthy volunteer has 12 independent tests, each with a 95% reference interval. What is the approximate chance that at least one result is flagged as outside its interval?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: 1 minus 0.95 to the power 12, which is about 0.46.
distractorRationale.b: This is the probability for a single test.
distractorRationale.c: This ignores the compounding of probabilities.
distractorRationale.d: This is the chance that one given test is within range, not the chance of a flag across 12 tests.

questions.explanation: The chance that all 12 are in range is 0.95 to the power 12, about 0.54. So the chance of at least one flag is about 0.46, or 46%.

questions.stem: A blood sample from a difficult venepuncture is visibly pink after centrifugation. Which result is most likely to be spuriously raised?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: red cells contain high potassium.

questions.explanation: Haemolysis releases intracellular contents. Potassium is about 20-fold higher inside red cells, so even mild lysis raises the measured value.

questions.stem: A 45-year-old well patient has potassium 8.6 mmol/L, calcium 1.2 mmol/L and a normal ECG and creatinine. Which explanation is most likely?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: EDTA adds potassium and chelates calcium and magnesium.
distractorRationale.b: This causes high calcium, not low.
distractorRationale.c: This does not explain the combination.
distractorRationale.d: Dilution would lower, not raise, potassium.

questions.explanation: Very high potassium with low calcium and no clinical or ECG features strongly suggests contamination from an EDTA tube. The test should be repeated on a fresh sample.

questions.stem: If the cut-off for calling a diagnostic test positive is raised, what is the expected effect?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: fewer false positives but more missed cases.
distractorRationale.b: This is the effect of lowering the cut-off.

questions.explanation: A stricter threshold labels fewer people as positive, so false positives fall (specificity rises) while true cases are missed more often (sensitivity falls).

questions.stem: The positive predictive value of a test depends on the prevalence of the disease in the population tested.
questions.explanation: For the same sensitivity and specificity, the proportion of positives that are true positives falls as the disease becomes rarer. This is why screening in a low-risk population produces many false positives.

questions.stem: A healthy reference population has a Gaussian distribution of an analyte with mean 140 mmol/L and standard deviation 2.5 mmol/L. Calculate the upper limit of the 95% reference interval in mmol/L using mean + 1.96 SD.
questions.explanation: The margin is 1.96 times 2.5, which is 4.9. Adding to the mean gives 144.9 mmol/L.

questions.stem: A test has sensitivity 90% and specificity 95% and is used in a population where disease prevalence is 2%. Calculate the positive predictive value as a percentage.
questions.explanation: In 1000 people, 20 have disease and 18 are detected; of 980 without disease, 5% or 49 are false positives. PPV is 18 divided by 67, which is about 26.9%.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old on a ward has a sample sent for urgent electrolytes. Potassium is reported as 7.1 mmol/L, yet the patient is well with a normal ECG. List the likely pre-analytical causes and describe what should be done.
markingGuide: Haemolysis from difficult venepuncture or traumatic collection
Delay in transport or separation causing leakage of potassium
Check the sample for haemolysis and the laboratory's haemolysis index
Repeat the test on a fresh, correctly collected sample
Treat the patient and not the number; consider clinical context and ECG
questions.explanation: The clinical picture does not fit the result, so a spurious result is likely. Marking should reward systematic identification and an action plan.

questions.stem: A new rapid test has sensitivity 98% and specificity 80% for a disease. Explain what these terms mean, which type of error each describes, and the value of the test for ruling disease in or out.
markingGuide: Sensitivity is the proportion of diseased people who test positive
Specificity is the proportion of non-diseased people who test negative
Low sensitivity gives false negatives; low specificity gives false positives
High sensitivity means a negative test is useful for ruling out
Specificity of 80% means many false positives and a positive needs confirmation
Positive predictive value depends on prevalence
A confirmatory test is needed after a positive result
questions.explanation: Sensitivity and specificity are properties of the test, but their clinical value depends on prevalence and the consequences of errors. Marking should reward correct definitions and clinical use.
